questions.q: Android, the mobile operating system, is built on which kernel?
questions.solution: Android uses the Linux kernel at its core with Java/Kotlin application layers on top - a standard exam fact.

questions.q: Which shortcut key runs the spelling and grammar check in MS Word?
questions.solution: F7 opens Spelling & Grammar. F5 opens Find & Replace's Go To (and starts a PowerPoint show), F9 refreshes fields, F12 is Save As.
questions.shortcut: F7 = spell-check in every Office app.

questions.q: Which tool **lists all installed hardware along with its drivers** and flags devices that are not working?
questions.solution: **Device Manager** enumerates every hardware component with its driver status — problem devices show a warning mark.

questions.q: In the extension .docx, the letter X stands for —
questions.solution: The X marks the **Office Open XML** format introduced with Office 2007 — the same X appears in .xlsx and .pptx.

questions.q: Select the word which is most opposite in meaning to the given word.  ACCEPT
questions.solution: Complementary pair: accept ↔ **refuse**. 'Except' only looks like 'accept' — a spelling trap, not an opposite.

questions.q:
Select the option that is OPPOSITE in meaning to the given idiom.

To be in someone's good books
options: to be out of favour with someone
questions.solution: *Be in someone's good books* = to be in their favour. Opposite: **out of favour** with them. 'Liked by someone' repeats the meaning.

questions.q: In the passage, the word 'redundant' most nearly means:
questions.solution: Critics believed the internet had made 'buildings full of books redundant' — unnecessary, a thing whose job was over; the next sentence ('The prediction has aged badly') confirms that critics expected libraries to become useless. So redundant = **(d) outdated and no longer needed**. (a) cost is never linked to the word. (b) plays on the idea of duplicate copies, which the passage does not discuss. (c) 'protected by law' has nothing to do with the critics' claim.
questions.shortcut: Antonym/synonym-in-context: plug your own word ('unnecessary') into the sentence first, then match; ignore options sharing nearby letters or images.
questions.passage:
There was a time when critics announced the death of the public library, confident that the internet had made buildings full of books redundant. The prediction has aged badly. Borrowing of printed books may have dipped in some cities, but library buildings are busier than they were a generation ago — because they have quietly become something more than warehouses for novels. In towns where a cup of coffee costs more than many can spare, the library remains the last indoor public space where no purchase is expected and no one asks you to leave.

Walk into any well-run city library this afternoon and you will find schoolchildren finishing homework at long tables, an unemployed man drafting job applications with a librarian's help, an elderly widow reading newspapers she cannot afford to subscribe to, and a coding club teaching teenagers in a side room. Librarians now spend as much time helping residents access government forms and digital services as they do recommending books.

This evolution has not been painless. Budgets trimmed by municipal councils force difficult choices between opening hours and new acquisitions, and smaller branches in poorer neighbourhoods — precisely those that need them most — are often the first to be marked for closure. Yet the case for investment has rarely been stronger. A society that worries about loneliness, digital exclusion and unequal schooling already owns an institution that addresses all three, staffed by professionals trained to help. The library needs not nostalgia but recognition: it is not a relic of the print age barely surviving; it is one of the few public institutions succeeding in both worlds.

questions.q: Parts of a sentence are given as options in order. One part contains an error; the other three are correct. Select the part with the error.
questions.solution: **Two days ago** is a finished time → simple past: Ravi **left** for Hyderabad two days ago. The present perfect refuses 'ago'.
questions.shortcut: ago → simple past, never has left.

questions.q: **Night blindness** is an early sign of the deficiency of —
questions.solution: **Vitamin A (retinol)** — carrots and papaya are rich sources; advanced lack causes xerophthalmia and corneal damage.

questions.q: A temperature of **50 °C** on the Kelvin scale is (take 0 °C = 273 K) —
questions.solution: K = C + 273 = 50 + 273 = **323 K**. (Subtracting gives 223, a common slip.)

questions.q: The **Pygmies**, known as forest dwellers of short stature, live in the:
questions.solution: **Pygmies** - equatorial rainforests of the **Congo basin**. Bushmen - Kalahari; Masai - East African savanna; Tuaregs - Sahara.

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, the **north-east trade winds** blow:
options: From the equatorial low towards the subtropical high
From west to east at 35-60 degrees
From the subtropical high towards the equatorial low
questions.solution: Trades flow out of the subtropical highs towards the Doldrums, deflected to become **north-east trades** in the north and **south-east trades** in the south.

questions.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a 30 m high tower from a point on the ground is $60^\circ$. The distance of the point from the base of the tower is:
questions.solution: $\tan60^\circ=\frac{30}{d}\Rightarrow\sqrt3=\frac{30}{d}\Rightarrow d=\frac{30}{\sqrt3}=10\sqrt3$ m.
questions.shortcut: 60° → distance $=\frac{h}{\sqrt3}=10\sqrt3$ m. Trap: $30\sqrt3$ (that is the 30° rule).

questions.q: 45 is what per cent of 360?
Which of the two numbers is greater: $\sqrt[3]{4}$ or $\sqrt[4]{6}$?
A shopkeeper allows a discount of 25% on the marked price and still gains 20%. The marked price is what per cent above the cost price?
questions.shortcut: 45% simply adds 20 + 25; the discount eats into the markup.

questions.q:
Select the term that can replace the question mark (?) in the following series.

**D5, G10, ?, M20, P25**
questions.solution: Letters D, G, _, M, P (+3) → J. Numbers 5, 10, _, 20, 25 (+5) → 15. Answer **J15**.
questions.shortcut: Both tracks pass through the gap evenly.

questions.q:
Find the missing number:

**12   23   53**

**31   14   54**

**21   32   ?**
questions.solution: Reverse each input, then add: 21 + 32 = 53 ✓; 13 + 41 = 54 ✓. So 12 + 23 = **35**. (53 adds the unreversed inputs — which is exactly row 1's output, a planted trap.)
questions.shortcut: Outputs look like sums of flipped numbers → reverse first.

questions.q: In a survey, **70% of people watch cricket, 60% watch football and 40% watch both.** What percentage watch **neither**?
questions.shortcut: Percentages behave exactly like counts — total is 100.

questions.q: The figure shows the **mirror image** of a wall clock (the dot marks 12). What is the actual time?
questions.solution: The dot marks 12. Read the picture as it is: the hands show **10:15**. That is the mirror image, so the actual time = 11:60 − 10:15 = **1:45**. Check: 10:15 + 1:45 = 12:00.
questions.shortcut: Read the picture, then subtract from 11:60.
